name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

name: AdaptSize
baseline: LRU (via unmodified Varnish Cache, a concurrent-LRU CDN memory cache with no admission control)
workload: Production CDN edge-cache trace replay comparing an unmodified Varnish Cache deployment against Varnish patched with the AdaptSize size-and-popularity-aware admission policy
claimed_speedup: AdaptSize achieves a 0.66 hit ratio vs 0.42 for unmodified Varnish (1.57x improvement), and stabilizes hit ratio variability (coefficient of variation 5% vs 23%, a 4.6x improvement), with no added throughput overhead (scales identically to unmodified Varnish)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.4.7 (specific optimization flags not stated)
hardware: FUJITSU CX250 HPC servers, dual Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPUs, 32GB RAM, RHEL 6.5 / kernel 2.6.32, IB QDR networking
tradeoffs: Proof-of-concept quality, not production-ready per its own README; admission-only policy (still relies on Varnish's own LRU eviction); needs periodic re-solving of its size-to-admission-probability model
caveats: Compiler version is stated (gcc 4.4.7) but exact optimization flags are not, so capped at tier B rather than A; production-trace comparison is against Varnish specifically, not raw textbook LRU or memcached/Redis
found_via: gh api users/dasebe/repos; gh api repos/dasebe/AdaptSize/readme; NSDI'17 paper PDF

name: Cacheus
workload: 17,766 simulation experiments over FIU, MSR and CloudPhysics block-storage traces at varying cache sizes, comparing hit rate against ARC, LIRS, DLIRS and LeCaR
claimed_speedup: Cacheus (using SR-LRU + CR-LFU experts) is statistically significantly better than ARC/LIRS/DLIRS/LeCaR in the majority of paired t-tests across 17,766 experiments; best-case improvement of 38.32% higher hit rate than ARC (CloudPhysics trace, 10% cache size); worst case is a 15.12% hit-rate degradation vs DLIRS (MSR trace, 5% cache size)
license: reference (no LICENSE file found in repo)
tradeoffs: Not uniformly better than every competitor (worst case is a real hit-rate loss vs DLIRS); adaptive combination of multiple experts (ARC/LIRS/LFU-style) adds bookkeeping overhead vs plain LRU; reference Python implementation is a research prototype, not built for production throughput (a C port exists inside libCacheSim)
caveats: Pure trace-driven simulation, no throughput/latency numbers or hardware given; repo has no OSI license file so treated as reference-only for reuse
found_via: gh search repos 'cacheus'; FAST'21 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

name: GL-Cache
workload: Production CDN/KV traces replayed through a Memcached-like prototype on CloudLab, measuring both hit ratio and throughput; group-level (not per-object) learned eviction
claimed_speedup: GL-Cache achieves 64% higher throughput than LRB (the prior object-level learned cache) at similar hit ratio; paper's evaluation table also reports GL-Cache beating LRU and size-aware Belady baselines directly, though the exact LRU-relative percentage is not isolated in the text we extracted
hardware: CloudLab Utah site m510 nodes: Intel Xeon D-1548 and Intel Xeon Gold 6142, 384GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Batches evictions over object groups instead of single objects, trading some eviction precision for far lower learning/inference overhead than object-level learned caches (e.g. LRB)
caveats: The clearest quantified comparison in the extracted text is against LRB, not literally against raw LRU/memcached; less exercised code path than the core libCacheSim algorithms (opt-in build flag)
found_via: junchengyang.com publication page; libCacheSim README algorithm list

name: Hyperbolic Caching
workload: Django-Wiki and NodeJS web applications using a modified Redis (forked at 3.0) as a look-aside cache, replaying Wikipedia (Jan 2008) and synthetic cost-aware workloads; also Memcachier-style trace-driven miss-rate simulation
claimed_speedup: Hyperbolic caching (random-sampling-based priority eviction) improves end-to-end application throughput by ~5-10% over default Redis while also lowering miss rate; e.g. NodeJS-over-Redis benchmark: throughput 10.0 vs 11.3 req/ms and miss rate 0.33 vs 0.27 for default vs Hyperbolic Redis (11.6% throughput gain in that run)
hardware: Rack of servers with Intel Xeon E5620 @ 2.40GHz CPUs
tradeoffs: Priority function needs periodic re-scaling/rebalancing as cost or popularity distributions shift; implemented as a ~380-line patch to Redis's existing random-sampling eviction rather than a new data structure, so gains are workload-dependent (competitive with, not always better than, ARC on cost-free workloads)
caveats: Repo is archived; GitHub reports its dominant language as Python (benchmark/harness scripts) even though the core change is a small C patch to Redis -- confirmed by the paper's own '380 lines of code' description of the Redis patch
found_via: ATC'17 paper PDF (usenix.org); paper's own code citation to github.com/kantai/hyperbolic-caching

name: LHD (Least Hit Density) / RankCache
workload: Commercial Memcachier and enterprise storage (MSR) traces simulated for hit-rate/space comparisons; RankCache, an LHD-based memcached-derived KV-cache, benchmarked for request throughput at up to 16 threads
claimed_speedup: LHD needs on average 8x less cache space than LRU (and 2-3x less than other proposed policies) to match the same hit rate; RankCache needs no synchronization in the common case, improving request throughput at 16 threads by 8x over LRU and 2x over CLOCK
hardware: Not stated in the extracted paper text for the RankCache throughput experiment
license: Custom MIT-style permissive license (Carnegie Mellon University; requests citation of the LHD paper, no patent grant)
tradeoffs: LHD's ranking function relies on modeling conditional-probability hit density which needs periodic reclassification/recomputation; the GitHub repo ships only the trace-driven simulator, not the RankCache memcached-based prototype used for the throughput numbers
caveats: The 8x/2x throughput-vs-LRU/CLOCK numbers are attributed to RankCache, a separate memcached-based prototype; the released CMU-CORGI/LHD repo is described by its own README as 'simulation code' only, so the throughput claim may not be independently reproducible from this exact repo
found_via: gh search repos 'LHD cache'; NSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: LRB (Learning Relaxed Belady) / webcachesim2
workload: CDN flash-cache prototype (built on Apache Traffic Server) replaying a 14-day Wikipedia production trace with a 1TB cache, plus simulations against LRU/LFUDA/TinyLFU/LeCaR/B-LRU at multiple cache sizes
claimed_speedup: LRB reduces average WAN bandwidth consumption by 44% and p95 bandwidth by 43% versus unmodified Apache Traffic Server (ATS, an LRU-based cache) at a 1TB flash cache size; simulations also place LRB's byte-miss-ratio ahead of LRU, LFUDA, TinyLFU and LeCaR across a range of cache sizes
hardware: 3x Google Cloud n1-standard-64 VMs (64 vCPUs, 240GB DRAM each) acting as client/proxy/origin, 8x375GB local NVMe combined via software RAID
stars_or_usage: 85 stars (companion prototype repo sunnyszy/lrb-prototype has 11 stars)
tradeoffs: Uses an online-trained ML model (~30us per inference) for eviction scoring, adding CPU overhead versus plain LRU (paper measures peak CPU 16% for LRB vs 9% for ATS at max throughput); needs a validation/warmup trace section to tune hyperparameters
caveats: Compiler/flags not stated in the extracted testbed section; throughput itself was essentially tied between LRB and ATS (11.72 vs 11.66 Gbps) -- the win is in bandwidth/miss-ratio, not raw request throughput
found_via: gh api users/sunnyszy/repos; gh search repos 'learning relaxed belady'; NSDI'20 paper PDF

name: MemC3
workload: Pre-generated YCSB-style key-value workload traces replayed against MemC3 and stock Memcached over the network to measure end-to-end query throughput and memory footprint for small key-value pairs; a separate local microbenchmark measures raw hash-table lookup throughput at 1 and 12 threads
claimed_speedup: Up to 3x the queries-per-second of stock Memcached on the same workload while using about 30% less memory for small key-value pairs (optimistic concurrent cuckoo hashing + CLOCK eviction combined); the core hash table alone reaches 5M lookups/sec at 1 thread and 35M lookups/sec at 12 threads
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz (2x6 cores), 2x12MB L3 cache, 2x16GB DDR3 RAM, 10Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: CLOCK-based eviction only approximates strict LRU, trading eviction precision for space/concurrency; cuckoo hashing needs load-factor headroom and can hit rare high-latency insert paths near capacity; the repo's own README says the successor project, libcuckoo, is the actively maintained re-engineering of MemC3's hash table
caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput/memory numbers, capping this at Tier B rather than A; the repo's own README notes the benchmark uses pre-generated YCSB-style traces rather than live YCSB; project unmaintained since 2017
found_via: GitHub: search 'memc3'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'13 session page and PDF (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MemC3: Compact and Concurrent MemCache with Dumber Caching and Smarter Hashing')

name: MICA
workload: Network GET/PUT benchmark over UDP/DPDK with tiny (8B key/8B value), small (16B/64B), and large (128B/1024B) items, uniform and Zipf(0.99)-skewed key popularity, 50% and 95% GET ratios, on a 16-core/8-partition server vs custom versions of Memcached, MemC3, Masstree, and RAMCloud
claimed_speedup: MICA reaches 65.6-76.9 Mops on tiny items (uniform and skewed); the next-best system (Masstree) tops out at 16.5 Mops, with Memcached/MemC3/RAMCloud all below 6.1 Mops on the same setup (>10x vs Memcached, >4x vs the next-fastest system overall); MICA's end-to-end latency is also lower and more stable as throughput rises versus original Memcached (Fig. 13, uniform 50% GET, tiny items)
hardware: Server: dual 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2680 @2.70GHz, 64GiB RAM (32GiB/NUMA node), 20MiB L3/CPU, eight 10Gb Ethernet ports (four Intel X520-T2 dual-port NICs); Clients: two machines with dual 6-core Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz and Intel X520-T2 NICs
license: Apache-2.0 (license text embedded in README; no separate LICENSE file in the repo)
tradeoffs: Requires Intel DPDK, hugepages, and a specific dual-socket/multi-NIC hardware layout to hit peak numbers; UDP-based protocol with no TCP or automatic loss recovery beyond GET/PUT idempotency; partitioned (EREW) design trades flexibility for scalability; cache mode uses a lossy, approximate-LRU hash index by design
caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput numbers, which is why this is capped at Tier B instead of A; repository unmodified since 2016 and targets DPDK 1.4.1-era APIs that will not build against modern DPDK without porting; license is only asserted in README text, not a LICENSE file
found_via: GitHub: search 'MICA key-value store'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'14 session page and PDF (Lim, Han, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MICA: A Holistic Approach to Fast In-Memory Key-Value Storage')

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

name: Pogocache
workload: memtier_benchmark 100K SET + 100K GET ops per client, 256 clients over 16 I/O threads, pipelining 1/10/25/50, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64), Unix socket, persistence off, 31 runs per point (median reported)
claimed_speedup: throughput ranking (pipeline 1, 8 threads): pogocache 3,145,960 ops/s vs memcache 2,601,306, garnet 1,548,050, dragonfly 1,407,584, valkey 1,331,683, redis 909,837 (~3.5x Redis, ~1.2x Memcached); lowest latency (111us) and fewest CPU cycles/op (6968) of the group
hardware: AWS c8g.8xlarge, 32-core non-NUMA ARM64
tradeoffs: Newer/less battle-tested than Redis/Memcached in production; supports Memcache, RESP and Postgres wire protocols but not full Redis command set (data structures, scripting, etc.)
caveats: The cache-benchmarks suite comparing pogocache to Redis/Valkey/Dragonfly/Garnet/Memcache is written and run by pogocache's own author (tidwall), so it is not a fully independent third party, even though the methodology (31 runs, median, stated hardware, stated versions) is unusually rigorous; exact compiler/build flags for each server are not listed, only released versions/commits
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tidwall/pogocache; README table pointing to linked cache-benchmarks repo, opened directly

name: RobinHood (tail-latency-aware cache repartitioning)
baseline: memcached-style per-backend caching without dynamic repartitioning
workload: 50-server production-trace testbed emulating a large web service (20 backend systems, memcached-compatible per-backend caches) under load spikes, measuring P99 request latency against a 150ms SLO
claimed_speedup: RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 latency goal 99.7% of the time during load spikes, versus only 70% of the time for the next-best static cache-partitioning policy tested
hardware: Servers provisioned with 2.4GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673v3
tradeoffs: Optimizes cross-backend cache-space allocation, not the per-cache eviction policy itself; requires a central resource-allocation (RBC) controller polling all backend caches, adding a coordination layer on top of plain memcached; reallocation decisions are rate-limited to avoid thrashing (ignores reallocations faster than 5s)
caveats: Baseline is 'next best' static/off-the-shelf cache partitioning across memcached-like backends, not literally raw memcached itself, so baseline_in_list is false and confidence is reduced accordingly; this is a cache resource-allocation system rather than a new eviction algorithm
found_via: gh api repos/dasebe/robinhoodcache/readme; OSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: S3-FIFO
workload: CacheLib-based KV-cache prototype replaying synthetic Zipf and production CDN/KV traces (CDN1, CDN2, Twitter, Meta), throughput scaling measured across 1-16 cores
claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU implementation in Meta's CacheLib at 16 cores; the gap widens further versus 2Q and TinyLFU; also reduces FIFO's miss ratio across most of the 1559 evaluated traces (see the paper's Fig.6-7 percentile plots)
hardware: CloudLab testbed nodes; the paper cites an AMD EPYC 9654P only as an example of a modern many-core CPU, not confirmed in the extracted text as the exact throughput-test machine
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); implemented inside Meta's CacheLib per the paper
tradeoffs: Uses three FIFO queues (small, main, ghost) instead of one list; ghost-queue metadata adds memory overhead; small-queue size ratio (S) needs tuning per workload
caveats: Exact CPU model for the throughput experiment and compiler/flags are not pinned down in the text we could extract, so capped at tier B not A
found_via: gh search repos 'S3-FIFO cache'; junchengyang.com publication page; arXiv search 'S3-FIFO cache eviction'

name: Segcache
workload: TTL-heavy small-object KV-cache workloads from Twitter production traces served through a Memcached-protocol-compatible server; measured in million queries/sec (MQPS) from 1 to 24 threads, and per-object metadata overhead
claimed_speedup: Up to 40% higher single-thread throughput than Memcached, close to 8x speedup over Memcached at 24 threads; 91% lower per-object metadata overhead than Memcached (down to ~5 bytes/object)
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230R CPU, 384GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Segment-based (not slab-based) memory management adds implementation complexity for highly variable object sizes; eviction/expiration happens at segment granularity rather than per-object
caveats: Memcached compared was v1.6.6 with segmented LRU (both scanning-enabled and disabled modes tested); paper text we extracted does not state the exact compiler/flags used to build either system
found_via: junchengyang.com publication page; gh api repos/Thesys-lab/Segcache

name: SIEVE
workload: 1559 CDN/KV traces (247B requests, Twitter/Meta/Wikimedia/proprietary CDN) replayed in libCacheSim for miss-ratio, plus a multi-threaded prototype cache replaying KV-cache workloads for throughput scaling from 1-16 threads
claimed_speedup: Prototype throughput is >2x an optimized 16-thread LRU (LRU plateaus at 4 threads while SIEVE keeps scaling); reduces mean miss ratio vs FIFO by 21% (up to 42% at p90) on CDN1 at large cache size, and vs ARC by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%, itself more than the 6.3% mean reduction ARC gets over LRU)
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6142 @ 2.6GHz, 384GB DDR4 DRAM (CloudLab c6420 node), turbo boost off, threads pinned within one NUMA node
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim, the reference implementation); promoted as production-ready on sievecache.com
tradeoffs: Needs a per-object 'visited' bit like CLOCK; underperforms TwoQ/LHD/ARC at very small cache sizes because new objects can't demonstrate popularity before being evicted
caveats: Paper states CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so capped at tier B; miss-ratio numbers come from libCacheSim simulation while the throughput numbers come from a separate hand-built prototype
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for 'SIEVE cache eviction'; junchengyang.com publication page; gh search repos 'SIEVE cache eviction'

name: Cachelot
workload: LRU cache benchmark: 2GB of random keys/values (1-4KB range) loaded into both Cachelot and Memcached under a 2GB memory limit each, measuring total 'effective memory' (surviving key/value bytes) retained
claimed_speedup: Cachelot keeps up to 15% more usable data than Memcached in the same RAM budget (per the cachelot.io benchmark page, with ~5-7% metadata overhead); README also states Cachelot 'is faster in terms of latency' but gives no latency numbers on the pages checked
tradeoffs: Single-threaded server design (scales via sharding/multiple processes, not one multithreaded process); fixed pre-allocated memory pool; only a subset of the memcached wire protocol
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or flags stated for the vs-Memcached benchmark; only a memory-efficiency percentage and a qualitative latency claim are given, with no independent verification; project has been stale since mid-2024
found_via: GitHub: search 'cachelot memcached' -> README's 'What is Cachelot Distributed Cache Server' section linking to the cachelot.io benchmarks page

name: Dragonfly
workload: memtier_benchmark SET/GET ops (-d 256) against Redis on m5.large/m5.xlarge, and against Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge; also idle/peak memory usage during BGSAVE-equivalent snapshot
claimed_speedup: up to 25x throughput vs a single Redis process on c6gn.16xlarge (3.8M QPS); ~4.8x SET QPS vs Memcached (3844K vs 806K) on c6gn.16xlarge; ~30% more memory efficient than Redis at idle
hardware: AWS m5.large, m5.xlarge, c6gn.16xlarge, r6g/c7g (instance types stated; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running it as a competing hosted service (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-11-01); single shared-nothing multi-threaded architecture differs operationally from Redis single-thread model
caveats: First-party README benchmark; AWS instance type given but exact CPU model, compiler, and build flags are not stated, so numbers cannot be independently reproduced from the README alone. A separate independent-ish suite (tidwall/cache-benchmarks) corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached on AWS c8g.8xlarge with stated versions (see the Pogocache entry in this file).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/dragonflydb/dragonfly (seeded from prior knowledge of 'modern replacement for Redis and Memcached'); README benchmarks section opened directly

name: IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)
workload: Multi-threaded client issuing blocking GET calls at fixed QPS levels (25K/50K/100K) against IKV (embedded, in-process) vs a 16-shard Redis Cluster on AWS ElastiCache; measuring avg/p50/p99 response time in microseconds
claimed_speedup: at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13us/p50 2.89us/p99 5.65us vs Redis Cluster avg 319us/p50 305us/p99 514us (roughly 100x lower average latency); README also claims embedded local Flash/SSD-backed IKV is still ~2x faster than an all-in-memory remote Redis cluster
tradeoffs: IKV is an embedded/in-process library colocated with the application (no network hop) rather than a shared remote cache, so much of the 100x gap is network round-trip elimination rather than a faster core engine; eventual consistency instead of Redis's stronger read-after-write guarantees; requires a separate data-plane (streams/object storage) to keep embedded replicas in sync
caveats: First-party README claim; linked full report is a Google Doc that could not be fully read in this session (only its title, 'IKV Perf Benchmarks | A comparison with Redis', was visible), so hardware/CPU model and compiler flags are unconfirmed; comparing an embedded cache against a networked cache is not entirely apples-to-apples for a 'faster engine' claim, though it is a legitimate real-workload latency win for the intended use case (ML feature serving)
found_via: HN Algolia: query 'faster than redis' -> 'IKV: embedded key-value store, 100x faster than Redis' (github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store); repo README opened directly

name: KeyDB
workload: memtier_benchmark, 32 threads over TLS, standard Redis GET/SET ops; benchmark client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), database instances on m5.4xlarge
claimed_speedup: over 7x faster than Redis with TLS enabled (~1M ops/s at 16 KeyDB threads vs ~130k ops/s for Redis 6 with TLS); Redis loses 36% throughput enabling TLS (61% with io-threads+TLS) while KeyDB shows almost no decline
hardware: AWS m5.8xlarge (client, 32 cores), m5.4xlarge (server instances) — CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Multithreading changes the concurrency/atomicity model vs Redis (MVCC-style access under a global lock for KEYS/SCAN); staying in sync with upstream Redis features is ongoing maintenance burden for a fork
caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance type stated but not exact CPU model, compiler, or build flags; repository has had no commits in ~2.5 years even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/Snapchat/KeyDB (seeded from prior knowledge of 'multithreaded fork of Redis'); README benchmark link opened directly

name: RAMCloud
workload: Remote object read/write over a datacenter network via RAMCloud's own low-latency RPC stack, contrasted qualitatively with Memcached-style caches that must fall back to disk/flash on cache misses
claimed_speedup: Project overview states reads complete in as little as 5us and writes in under 15us, describing this as '10-1000x faster than other available alternatives' and explicitly contrasting with Memcached-style caches that must handle misses and disk/flash access
tradeoffs: Requires keeping the whole dataset in DRAM across a cluster (disk/flash used only for backup logging), unlike Memcached's standalone cache-aside model; needs a full cluster (coordinator + masters + backups) rather than a single process; lowest latencies assume InfiniBand/kernel-bypass transport
caveats: The 5us/15us and '10-1000x' figures appear on the project's own wiki overview page without a stated CPU model, compiler, or reproducible benchmark harness on that page (Tier C, not A/B); '10-1000x' reads as a general marketing figure rather than a specific measured ratio against Memcached; project is explicitly marked no longer maintained, last commit 2019
found_via: GitHub: search 'RAMCloud' (cross-referenced from MICA paper's compared-systems list); RAMCloud project wiki 'What is RAMCloud?' overview page

name: RapidKV
workload: memtier_benchmark against RapidKV and Redis on the same machine (CPU-pinned via taskset): baseline pipeline=1, 1:1 SET:GET, 8B values, 100K keys; realistic pipeline=16, 1:9 SET:GET, 64B values, 200K keys; and a pipeline-depth sweep (1/10/100) at 1:9 SET:GET, 8B values, 1M keys, 30s runs
claimed_speedup: At pipeline=1 throughput is within 4% (135,165 vs 130,019 ops/sec) but p99 latency is 49% lower; at pipeline=16 mixed workload RapidKV is +63% ops/sec (1,823,366 vs 1,119,012) with 58% lower p99; at pipeline=100 RapidKV reaches 5,178,742 vs Redis's 1,718,018 ops/sec, a 3.01x speedup; author's headline figure is 'up to ~4.2x faster than Redis on pipelined workloads' (pipeline=500)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 4800H (8C/16T, 2.9GHz base), 16GB RAM, 32KiB L1d/L1i x8, 512KiB L2 x8, 4096KiB L3 x2, Kubuntu 24.04 LTS
tradeoffs: Single-threaded, no multi-core scaling; implements only a small subset of Redis commands (PING/ECHO/SET/GET/DEL/EXISTS/INCR/DECR/INCRBY/DECRBY/EXPIRE/PERSIST/TTL - no lists/hashes/sets/pub-sub/persistence/replication); SIEVE eviction approximates LRU rather than exact LRU
caveats: First-party, self-run benchmark with no independent verification and no compiler/flags stated (Tier C); only 1 GitHub star and first commits in 2026, so track record is minimal; the 4.2x headline is the best case at pipeline=500, not representative of the near-parity no-pipeline case
found_via: GitHub: search 'faster than Redis' language:C++

name: W-TinyLFU (C++ header-only, based on the TinyLFU paper)
workload: Synthetic Zipf(0.7/0.94) and SPC1-like traces plus real YouTube/Wikipedia/DS1/S3/OLTP traces evaluated for hit ratio, comparing TinyLFU-admission-augmented LRU/Random/LFU against plain LRU, ARC, SLRU, LRU-K and others (algorithm's own paper; this specific repo is an independent C++11 header-only reimplementation)
claimed_speedup: W-TinyLFU matches or beats every other evaluated policy's hit ratio on every tested trace ('the only scheme to obtain such good results on all traces' per the paper); e.g. reduces the frequency-sketch memory needed versus a naive counting approach by ~89% in the reported Zipf-0.9 experiment
tradeoffs: This specific repo explicitly omits thread-safety and hash-collision protection ('barebones' header-only port); the underlying TinyLFU paper's hit-ratio numbers come from a Java prototype and from Caffeine, not from this C++ port directly
caveats: The quantitative hit-ratio claims are from the original paper's Java/Caffeine evaluation, not independently re-measured against this specific C++ header-only port, so this is tier C for this repo despite the algorithm's own paper being well cited; Caffeine itself (the canonical TinyLFU implementation) is already catalogued and excluded

name: BtrBlocks
baseline: Apache Parquet (generated/read via the Apache Arrow C++ library) and Apache ORC
workload: In-memory decompression throughput and S3 cold-column-scan dollar-cost, measured on the 5 largest Public BI Benchmark datasets (~2451 columns) and all 22 TPC-H queries.

Scanning individual columns from S3 is 9x cheaper than compressed Parquet variants and 20x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet on average; across all 22 TPC-H queries, Parquet/Parquet+Snappy/Parquet+Zstd cost 5.5x/3.6x/2.8x more than BtrBlocks.

A later, separate VLDB 2025 paper (FastLanes File Format, by an overlapping CWI research community) independently re-ran BtrBlocks on different hardware (AWS i4i.4xlarge) and found it 7x slower decoding/encoding than FastLanes, close to Parquet+Zstd's compression ratio, unable to benefit from AVX512, and could not be adapted for true single-value random access without a full API reimplementation -- weakening BtrBlocks' relative standing versus newer formats even though its original Parquet/ORC comparison holds up.

name: FastLanes
baseline: DuckDB (also compared against Apache Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd)
workload: Decoding/encoding throughput (rowgroups/sec) across real-world datasets and a single-value random-access latency micro-benchmark, comparing the FastLanes file format against DuckDB, Parquet+Snappy, Parquet+Zstd, and BtrBlocks.
claimed_speedup: On average 29x faster decoding/encoding throughput than DuckDB, 43x than Parquet+Snappy, 44x than Parquet+Zstd, 7x than BtrBlocks (Table 4); for single-value random access, 5x faster than DuckDB, 315x than Parquet+Snappy, 416x than Parquet+Zstd, 800x than BtrBlocks (Table 5)

caveats: The headline multipliers are from the FastLanes authors' own VLDB 2025 paper ("The FastLanes File Format"), not an independent third party, though methodology, hardware, and compiler flags are fully documented and code is public, satisfying tier A. The random-access micro-benchmark used different hardware (Apple M4) than the main Ice Lake throughput benchmark, so those two numbers are not directly comparable to each other.

name: Lance
workload: Random-access point lookups and full-scan throughput on NVMe-backed storage, per the VLDB 2025 paper 'Lance: Efficient Random Access in Columnar Storage through Adaptive Structural Encodings' (hardware: NVMe drive + Intel i7-10700K, 8 cores/16 threads).
claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing claim: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper is more nuanced: its own abstract states 'Parquet, when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' -- i.e. most of the headline 100x gap is against Parquet's poorly-tuned defaults, not a well-tuned Parquet baseline; Lance's actual claimed contribution is matching/exceeding well-tuned Parquet's random access without giving up scan throughput or RAM usage.
hardware: NVMe drive with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the VLDB 2025 paper
tradeoffs: Rust-native with Python/Java bindings (pylance); optimized for AI/ML lakehouse workloads (multimodal blobs, vector indexes, data versioning) rather than general OLAP scans; file format still evolving under a data_storage_version compatibility contract.
caveats: The widely repeated '100x faster than Parquet' figure is a marketing headline (README/homepage), not a number found stated verbatim in the peer-reviewed paper; the paper itself undercuts the headline by showing well-tuned Parquet already recovers most (60x) of that gap versus default Parquet settings, so this is downgraded from the vendor's implied claim to tier C pending a clean apples-to-apples number against tuned Parquet.

name: StarRocks
workload: Star Schema Benchmark (SSB), 13 queries on flat tables (vendor blog post dated Aug 21, 2023)
claimed_speedup: "ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks" on SSB (vendor blog; hardware/compiler not stated in the post)
tradeoffs: MPP architecture with a separate Java frontend (FE, planner/metadata) and C++ backend (BE, vectorized execution engine) -- heavier operational footprint than embedded engines like DuckDB; MySQL-wire compatible.
caveats: The 2.2x claim is from StarRocks' own 2023 blog post with no hardware/CPU model or compiler flags stated (tier C). It is directly CONTRADICTED by ClickHouse's own independent, reproducible ClickBench suite: on identical c6a.4xlarge hardware, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run totals 18.03s (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 ClickBench queries) versus StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run at 44.47s -- i.e. ClickHouse is now roughly 2.5x FASTER than StarRocks on ClickBench, the reverse of the vendor's SSB claim (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo, clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). The discrepancy likely reflects ~3 years of ClickHouse improvements plus workload differences (SSB star-schema joins vs. ClickBench's flat-table scans), but it substantially weakens confidence in the vendor claim as a current, general statement.

name: BVLSM
workload: 64KB random-write big-value workloads against RocksDB v9.7.3 and BlobDB, WAL-time key-value separation vs RocksDB's flush-time separation
claimed_speedup: 7.6x over RocksDB and 1.9x over BlobDB in one experiment; ~7x and 3x speedups over RocksDB reported elsewhere in the paper
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16C/32T, 2.30GHz), Samsung 990 EVO NVMe SSD (1TB), Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Separates key/value at WAL-write time rather than at flush time so MemTables only hold lightweight metadata; adds a multi-queue BValue store and BVCache; targets big-value (multimedia/embedding) workloads specifically, smaller advantage expected for small-value workloads typical of many RocksDB deployments.
caveats: cs.DB preprint on arXiv with no journal-ref found (not confirmed peer-reviewed as of this search) and no public code repository located, so capped at tier C; first-party benchmark numbers only.

name: Mycelium (TE-LSM)

caveats: No public code repository found; not confirmed peer-reviewed within this session (no journal-ref in arXiv metadata); first-party benchmark only, hence tier C. The reported gain applies specifically to certain query types layered atop compaction, not general point-lookup throughput.

name: Nova-LSM

caveats: Compiler/build flags are not stated in the paper; the single-node HDD-based hardware is also fairly dated. One reported speedup (105x) exceeds the 50x implausibility threshold without documented compiler/flags, so tier is capped at C per hard rules even though code is public and most other hardware/methodology details are given. Not confirmed as peer-reviewed within this session (arXiv metadata carries no journal-ref).

name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used
tradeoffs: No concurrency support; amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost vs B+Tree's better worst case; needs periodic subtree adjustment; benefit shrinks a lot on highly non-uniform key distributions
caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only; gains vary strongly by dataset (as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset); repo unmaintained since Feb 2022

name: ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)
baseline: STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 4 real datasets (longitudes, longlat, lognormal, YCSB; 200M 8-byte keys) under read-only and read-write (mixed insert) workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K 3.6GHz, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
stars_or_usage: 701 stars; used as a baseline by many follow-up learned-index papers (LIPP, CARMI, etc.)
tradeoffs: No concurrency support in the public implementation; can degrade under adversarial/skewed insert patterns without retraining; README explicitly calls it 'a near drop-in replacement for std::map'
caveats: Hardware stated in the SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv preprint) but compiler/optimization flags not given in the accessible text; independently reused as a baseline by later peer-reviewed papers (LIPP, CARMI), which corroborate the B+Tree comparison
found_via: Starting query variation: 'in-memory learned index drop-in replacement std::map faster than B-tree'

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely

name: Bourbon (learned index for LSM-trees, OSDI'20 artifact)
workload: End-to-end lookup performance of a WiscKey/LevelDB-based LSM-tree modified to use per-file learned (piecewise-linear-regression) indexes, compared against unmodified state-of-the-art production LSM implementations.
claimed_speedup: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs."
tradeoffs: Learned index is trained per SSTable file at compaction time using a cost-benefit rule to decide when learning is worthwhile; benefits are workload/data-distribution dependent (helps most when keys within a file are well-approximated by a piecewise-linear model).
caveats: OSDI 2020 peer-reviewed paper (Tier B: hardware/compiler/flags were not visible on the fetched USENIX abstract page, only the headline speedup range). This GitHub repo is maintained by a third party as an artifact/course-project mirror of the original authors' (Yifan Dai et al.) code, not the original lab's own org; treat as a redistribution of the OSDI'20 artifact rather than an independent implementation.

name: Cuckoo Trie
workload: YCSB-C (100% lookup, uniform distribution) on the osm dataset (real-world key distribution, >=1GB index, exceeding LLC capacity), single-threaded, comparing the Cuckoo Trie against STX B-Tree, ARTOLC, HOT, and Wormhole.
claimed_speedup: "the Cuckoo Trie outperforms the other indexes—by up to 35% (HOT), 20% (ARTOLC), 50% (Wormhole) and 360% (STX) on YCSB-C with osm."
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (Skylake), 14 cores @ 2.6GHz per socket, 96GB DDR4-2666 per NUMA node, hyper-threading/Turbo-Boost disabled

Author states this implementation 'was created to run the experiments in the paper' and 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program' (README).

name: fast64 (FAST: Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, 64-bit)
workload: Point lookups (10M queries) over 200M 64-bit keys from the amzn SOSD dataset, comparing the FAST SIMD-friendly tree against a tuned STX B-Tree.
claimed_speedup: 435.33 ns/lookup (102.0 MB) for FAST vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree on amzn -> a modest ~1.1x lower latency at same-ish accuracy (derived from page data, Table 2); separately, FAST showed the highest multithreaded scaling of any structure tested, 32x throughput at 40 threads vs its own single-thread baseline.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM (20 physical / 40 logical cores for the multithreading experiment)
tradeoffs: Read-only, static tree built once; relies heavily on AVX-512 for its throughput and multithreaded scaling advantage, so results are CPU-generation dependent; build times are among the slowest of the structures SOSD tested.
caveats: The single-thread latency margin over STX B-Tree in Table 2 is small (~10%); the much larger 32x claim is a self-relative multithreading speedup, not a multithreaded FAST-vs-BTree comparison, so it is reported separately and should not be conflated with a 32x win over BTree.
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (fast64 -> RyanMarcus/fast64); numbers from SOSD VLDB'21 paper Table 2 and Section 4.5 (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

name: HOT (Height Optimized Trie)
workload: YCSB workload C (100% read) and workload E (95% short range-scan, 5% insert) over 50M-entry url/email/yago/integer key data sets, single node, comparing HOT against the STX B+-Tree, ART, and Masstree.
claimed_speedup: "For the lookup-only workload C, HOT achieves an at least 25% higher throughput across all evaluated data sets compared to the other evaluated index structures... In case of the URL data set, HOT's throughput is 200% higher than for the other data structures" (workload E).
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (4-core, 3.4GHz/4.0GHz turbo) and Intel i9-7900X (10-core, 3.3GHz/4.3GHz turbo)
tradeoffs: Header-only, order-preserving trie with a variable per-node bit span for balance; uses the most memory-efficient layout of the four structures tested in its own paper, but ART shows 50% higher insertion throughput than HOT on pure-integer keys; string-heavy tries (Masstree, ART) grow space 51-230% on long textual keys where HOT only grows 26%.
caveats: SIGMOD 2018 peer-reviewed paper: two CPU models and GCC 7.2 are stated, but optimization flags are not, capping this at Tier B. Repo has not been pushed to since 2018; treat as a finished/frozen academic artifact rather than an actively developed library.

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index); also matches a cache-efficient B+-tree and CSS-tree at far less space
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: PGM-index matches the fastest B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB) and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 83x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); at matched space, PGM-index dominates a 2-stage RMI in latency
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: VLDB'20 paper states hardware but not compiler/flags; the clear throughput/latency win over a named baseline is specifically vs RMI, while the B+-tree/CSS-tree comparisons are same-speed-less-space rather than strictly faster
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

name: PLEX / TrieSpline

name: Prefix Filter
workload: Space usage, false-positive rate, operation throughput at varying load, and build time for 0.94*2^28 (~252M) random 64-bit keys at false-positive rate ~2^-8, single-threaded, on an Intel Ice Lake server (PVLDB 15(7), 2022)
claimed_speedup: Overall build time faster than the vector quotient filter and cuckoo filter by 1.39-1.46x and 3.2-3.5x respectively; cuckoo filter's own insertion throughput collapses (a 27x slowdown observed) as occupancy approaches capacity, while prefix filter insertions stay fast; query throughput is comparable to (though about 52%/79% behind, for negative/positive queries) the cuckoo filter at low occupancy; far more space-efficient than the blocked Bloom filter at low target false-positive rates
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0, Ubuntu 20.04 (specific optimization flags beyond compiler version not stated in the extracted text)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) @ 2.40GHz, 64GiB RAM, 48KiB L1d/1.25MiB L2 per core, 36MiB shared L3
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware for the fast path; is an incremental filter (supports insertion but the paper focuses on a fixed configured capacity); this is a mixed win, not a strict speed win across every metric.
caveats: IMPORTANT: query throughput is NOT better than the cuckoo filter in this paper's own numbers -- the cuckoo filter is faster for queries at low occupancy (by 52%/79%). Prefix filter's real advantages are build/insertion time and avoiding cuckoo filter's occupancy-dependent insertion collapse, plus much better space efficiency than the blocked Bloom filter. Repo license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md though GitHub's own license detector reports NOASSERTION.

name: Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter)
workload: 192MB filters holding ~120-128M pre-generated 64-bit random-integer keys; lookup throughput measured while varying the fraction of positive queries, and insert throughput measured across load factor, on a two-socket Intel Xeon testbed.
claimed_speedup: Lookup throughput stays flat at ~11 MOPS for the cuckoo filter across all query mixes vs. Bloom filter dropping from ~8 MOPS (0% positive) to ~4 MOPS (100% positive) (Fig. 5, derived from page data: up to ~2.75x); cuckoo filter needs fewer bits/item than a space-optimized Bloom filter whenever target false-positive rate < 3% (crossover at 7.2 bits/item, Fig. 4); construction rate 5.00M keys/sec (CF) vs 3.91M keys/sec (BF) at 192MB (Table 3).
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @ 2.27GHz, 12MB L3 cache, 32GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Supports deletion unlike standard Bloom filters, but load factor caps insert capacity (~95% full before insert failures); asymptotically worse in bits/item (O(log n)) than Bloom's O(1), though practically better for realistic table sizes with reasonably sized buckets; duplicate-heavy workloads (same item inserted >2b times) can fail insertion.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ACM CoNEXT'14 paper (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, Mitzenmacher) states hardware but not compiler/flags, so capped at Tier B rather than A even though the benchmark harness (bulk-insert-and-query.cc, conext-figure5.cc, conext-table3.cc) is public in the repo's benchmarks/ dir. README itself carries no numbers; numbers above come from the paper.

name: Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter (PLBF)

name: SIMD Blocked Bloom Filter (src/simd-block.h, Impala-derived)
workload: Same 192MB-filter, ~124M-key benchmark as the cuckoo filter paper's evaluation; blocked (one-cache-line-per-item) Bloom filter vs. standard Bloom filter, construction rate and lookup throughput across varying positive-query fraction, two-socket Intel Xeon testbed.
